newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Expanding bureaucracy in Bosnia raises concerns.
newsitem.headline: Expanding bureaucracy in Bosnia raises concerns.

text.p: Postwar Bosnia is weighed down by a vast number of civil servants with dubious qualifications who are devouring big chunks of revenue at the expense of economic reconstruction, foreign experts said on Wednesday.

A team of analysts from the World Bank, U.S. Treasury Department and Agency for International Development (USAID) recently found that some 140,000 people were employed as civil servants in a country with a workforce of 1.3 million.
The investigation led by the World Bank reported an especially worrying trend in Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation, where 10 cantons govern with a large degree of autonomy.

"At the canton level there is a rather obscure criteria of hiring and firing and there is a tendency in certain cantons to hire large numbers of people without giving due weight to the need for the qualifications of these people," Rory O'Sullivan, director of the World Bank in Sarajevo, told Reuters.
The federation's cantons received some two billion German marks ($1.17 billion) in revenues last year, but much of the money has been devoted to hiring public employees, he said.

Concerned about burgeoning local bureaucracies in peacetime, the World Bank is drawing up recommendations to curb hiring policies and harmonise fiscal relations between the cantons and the central federation authorities, he said.

Western financial authorities say Bosnia risks squandering reconstruction opportunities by pouring money into public administration rather than projects to promote a revival of business and privatisation.
Bosnia's federation is an uneasy alliance of Moslems and Croats, founded in March 1994 through U.S. mediation.
The federation agreement accorded a large degree of political autonomy to the cantons, which has made for problems in the economic sphere, foreign experts said.
"The cantons were given tremendous power in passing legislation," said one expert, who asked not to be named.
"Basically, we created 10 mini-states and they are expanding their hiring without any regard for the big picture."
Each canton has its own assembly, government and judicial system which govern various municipalities.
Federation authorities were unavailable for comment.

In Bosnia's other entity, the Serb republic, some 35,000 people are employed as civil servants out of the country-wide total of 140,000. But foreign experts say unpaid salaries -- not hiring practises -- are the main problem in Serb territory.
Moslem-Croat and Serb territories are linked by a small central government, comprised of a three-man presidency, cabinet and parliament.
Although federation and Serb republic authorities have a multitude of civil servants at their disposal, the central state bodies have skeletal staffs, O'Sullivan said.

"The fact is the joint institutions are just the minister and his two deputies, with nobody else working for them. Clearly, this is a tremendous concern because the state is not a viable state until it has viable joint institutions."
